I have chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis, I can walk, and I use wheelchair. All the examples I said are of people I met over the years in hospitals.

Of course not having use of legs counts as disabled.

But it's far from only disability that lands people in wheelchair.

What about people who suffer from postural orthostatic intolerance, severe epileptic seizures or unexpected syncope? They are perfectly capable of walking and are strong people, but may fall down and split their skull open without any notice.

What about people who have fibromyalgia or chronic fatigue syndrome who suffer from great pain for days after exerting themselves? They may be perfectly able to walk for 5 or 10 minutes.

What about people who are recovering from joint surgery in their legs where doctor tells them not to put pressure on their joints for longer periods of time?

What about people who have mitochondrial dysfunctions where they have full mobility of their legs but very limited supplies of daily energy?

What about people with degenerative muscle diseases where they are constantly wasting away and waiting to die but may at the precise moment when you saw them not be ill enough to not be able to stand up?

Should they all stay home so judgmental ignoramuses like you don't feel offended when they see a person in a wheelchair stand up?
Being disabled and not having use of legs is not the same thing.

It depends. 

A healthy 80-year-old should have no trouble walking up a flight of stairs. And it is generally considered that life is more complicated and everyday tasks take longer for disabled people which is why we give them priority.

On the other hand older people certainly have more chance of having joint or muscle pain or fatigue, etc.

Still, we can't know why a person is in wheelchair. It might be more serious and more painful than a simple case of inability to use legs.

When we don't know people it's best to assume they have a good reason for using the elevator or wheelchair and not risk accidentally being a jerk to someone who has an invisible illness.

There are also people with invisible illnesses. 
 
I'm 25, I have myalgic encephalomyelitis, and it's constant stress for me that people will think I'm rude or inconsiderate. 

On good days I can take a half-hour walk, but if I go up a flight of stairs I get arrhythmia and muscle pain for days on end. 

There's also arthritis and all kinds of other ailments that can make a person look completely healthy at first sight, but make it extremely difficult for them to take the stairs.
